historical_timeline.summary: Graduated from the Pennsylvania College of Dental Surgery and began practicing dentistry in Atlanta.
Diagnosed with tuberculosis and advised to move to a drier climate.
Died of tuberculosis in Glenwood Springs, Colorado.

claims.statement: John Henry Holliday was born on August 14, 1851, in Griffin, Georgia.
In 1866 Holliday's mother died of tuberculosis.
He enrolled at the Pennsylvania College of Dental Surgery in 1870 and graduated in 1872, then practiced dentistry in Atlanta before opening his own practice in Griffin.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports his occupation as a newly qualified dentist in the modern episode.

claims.statement: Shortly after beginning his career as a dentist in Atlanta he developed a bad cough; doctors diagnosed tuberculosis and advised a move to a more arid climate. He developed chronic pulmonary tuberculosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchor for the modern pulmonary tuberculosis.

claims.statement: He was diagnosed with tuberculosis in 1873 and moved west for a healthier, drier climate, arriving in Dallas, Texas, in September 1873.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Dates the diagnosis; the episode's true frame ends before the move.

claims.statement: He made his living at the card tables, aggravating his tuberculosis with heavy drinking and late nights.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchor for the modern alcohol use disorder; the source does not date the heavy drinking.

claims.statement: He died of tuberculosis in its final stages on November 8, 1887, in Glenwood Springs, Colorado, at the age of 36.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded as a fact; the modern episode ends with cure.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Diagnosis and six-month treatment of drug-susceptible cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis in a 21-year-old dentist under the ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline (three sputum smears, nucleic acid amplification, culture and susceptibility, HIV and hepatitis testing, baseline liver tests and vision checks, isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for eight weeks then isoniazid and rifampin for eighteen weeks by video-observed therapy, stopping ethambutol on susceptibility results, monthly liver and symptom monitoring, release from isolation, two-month culture conversion, contact investigation, and public-health reporting), together with care for an alcohol use disorder that raises the risk of isoniazid liver injury (AUDIT, brief intervention, counseling, and a structured safety assessment with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), and an honest account of a liver-monitoring gap.

documentation.chief_complaint: Two-week follow-up on tuberculosis treatment, seen the same day by infectious diseases

hpi.narrative: Mr. Holliday is a 21-year-old dentist with cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis who returns two weeks after diagnosis and is seen by infectious diseases today. He started isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and pyridoxine two days after the first visit, once the nucleic acid amplification test confirmed tuberculosis, and has taken all thirteen doses on daily video calls with the health department nurse. His cough is less frequent, the blood streaks in his sputum have stopped, and the night sweats are lighter. He has mild nausea in the hour after the morning doses, eased by taking them at bedtime with a small snack. His urine and tears are orange, as he was warned. He has no yellowing, dark urine, abdominal pain, rash, numbness, or change in vision or color. He is isolating at home and not working; his roommate is being tested by the health department. He has cut down to a drink or two on three evenings in the two weeks and has not played cards. He feels low about being away from his practice but has no thoughts of suicide.

assessment_plan.assessment: Early clinical response and full adherence. Baseline sputum cultures are growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex; susceptibility results are pending. Infectious diseases agrees with the standard regimen and plan

Three sputum samples on consecutive mornings in one week for the release decision
Stop ethambutol once the isolate is shown to be susceptible to isoniazid and rifampin
Liver tests monthly throughout treatment; stop the doses and call the same day for hepatitis symptoms

hpi.narrative: Mr. Holliday returns five weeks into treatment. The isolate is susceptible to isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, and ethambutol was stopped a week ago when the result arrived. The three sputum smears collected in the third week were negative, and with his clinical improvement and more than two weeks of treatment he was released from home isolation two weeks ago and returned to work the following week. His cough is now occasional and dry, and the night sweats have stopped. He has taken every dose by video. He has no nausea now, no yellowing, dark urine, abdominal pain, numbness, or vision change. He has not had a drink in three weeks and has met his counselor twice. His roommate's first blood test was negative and will be repeated by the health department.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Holliday is a 21-year-old dentist with drug-susceptible cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis in the sixth week of the continuation phase of isoniazid and rifampin, given by video-observed therapy, and with a mild alcohol use disorder. Two days ago he developed nausea and loose stools, and he vomited twice yesterday; two coworkers at the dental office had a stomach illness last week. When he reported the nausea on his video call this morning, the health department nurse told him to hold today's doses, as his treatment plan instructs, and to be seen today with liver tests. He has no yellowing of the eyes or skin, no dark urine or pale stools, no pain under the right ribs, and no itching or rash. His cough has gone and he has had no fevers or night sweats. He has not missed any other dose. He told us that nine days ago, at a friend's birthday party, he drank about six whiskeys over an evening, the first time he has drunk heavily since starting treatment; he has not drunk since. He feels he let himself down but has no thoughts of suicide.

referral.question: New cavitary, smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis in a 21-year-old dentist who drinks heavily. Please confirm the regimen and doses, advise on liver monitoring given his alcohol use, and advise on isolation, return to dental work, and the length of treatment
referral.urgency: Urgent, within two weeks, on the same day as his two-week primary care visit
referral.pertinent_history: Two months of cough, blood-streaked sputum, night sweats, and weight loss to 58.0 kg (BMI 18.3); temperature 37.8 °C, oxygen saturation 95 percent. Chest X-ray: right upper lobe consolidation with a 3 cm cavity. First sputum smear for acid-fast bacilli 2+ today; two early-morning samples to follow, and a nucleic acid amplification test, culture, and susceptibility testing ordered. HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C tests sent. Baseline ALT 34, AST 38, bilirubin 0.6, GGT 78 (high), albumin 3.4 (low), hemoglobin 12.6 (low), platelets 412 (high), HbA1c 5.2, creatinine 0.86. Visual acuity 85 letters in each eye with normal color vision. Alcohol: AUDIT 15, whiskey four or more evenings a week, often six or more drinks, mostly at late-night card games; mild alcohol use disorder; brief intervention given; safety assessment with no current risk. No other medicines; no known allergies. Plan: isoniazid 300 mg, rifampin 600 mg, pyrazinamide 1500 mg, ethambutol 1200 mg, and pyridoxine 50 mg daily by video-observed therapy with the health department, starting as soon as the amplification test confirms tuberculosis. Reported to the health department today; isolating at home
questions: Do you agree with the regimen and the weight-based doses?
How should his liver be monitored, given his drinking, and when should the drugs be stopped?
When can he leave home isolation and return to treating patients?
How long should treatment last, given the cavity, and is the four-month rifapentine and moxifloxacin regimen an option?
Is any other testing or follow-up needed from infectious diseases?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Holliday, a 21-year-old dentist, is seen at the request of Dr. Beaumont two weeks after a diagnosis of cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis. He has taken all thirteen doses of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol with pyridoxine by video-observed therapy. His cough and night sweats are improving and the hemoptysis has stopped. He has mild nausea after the morning doses and orange urine and tears, and no jaundice, abdominal pain, rash, numbness, or vision change. He has cut his drinking down sharply. He has no travel outside the country, no known contact with drug-resistant tuberculosis, and no immune-suppressing condition or medicine
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Beaumont's diagnostic note; the chest X-ray; the three baseline smears and the nucleic acid amplification result; today's report that the baseline cultures are growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, with susceptibility pending; the HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C results, all negative, with no hepatitis B immunity; and today's liver tests and vision check

exam.finding: Thin; temperature 37.3 °C, heart rate 92; seen in a negative-pressure room
No icterus; visual acuity and color vision normal
Coarse crackles and bronchial breathing over the right upper zone

assessment.assessment: Smear-positive, culture-positive cavitary disease with an early clinical response and full adherence. No rifampin resistance on the molecular test; isoniazid susceptibility is pending. The regimen and the weight-band doses are correct: isoniazid about 5 mg/kg, rifampin about 10 mg/kg, pyrazinamide 1500 mg and ethambutol 1200 mg for 56 to 75 kg. HIV negative

Heavy drinking, low albumin, and the three hepatotoxic drugs together raise his risk of drug-induced liver injury. Today's ALT 41, AST 39, and bilirubin 0.7 are normal. Injury is defined as ALT at least three times the upper limit with symptoms, or at least five times without symptoms, or a bilirubin rise; small rises below this are common and do not need the drugs stopped

He remains infectious until he has three negative sputum smears, a clinical response, and at least two weeks of effective treatment. Because he works close to patients' faces, return should wait for all three

Six months in total if the two-month culture is negative. A cavity on the first X-ray together with a positive two-month culture would extend the continuation phase to seven months. The four-month rifapentine and moxifloxacin regimen is an alternative only at the start of treatment; switching now offers no benefit

Stopping alcohol is the most useful thing he can do for his liver during treatment. If medication is wanted, acamprosate is preferred, because it is not processed by the liver; naltrexone and disulfiram are best avoided while he is on hepatotoxic drugs

recommendations: Continue isoniazid 300 mg, rifampin 600 mg, pyrazinamide 1500 mg, ethambutol 1200 mg, and pyridoxine 50 mg daily by video-observed therapy, seven days a week, for the 56-dose intensive phase; bedtime dosing with a snack for the nausea
Stop ethambutol once the isolate is shown to be susceptible to isoniazid and rifampin
Visual acuity and color vision monthly while on ethambutol

Liver tests monthly throughout treatment because of his drinking, and at once for any nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice, or dark urine; the health department nurse should hold doses for those symptoms until results are back
Stop all hepatotoxic drugs if ALT reaches three times the upper limit with symptoms, or five times without, and call me
Three sputum smears on consecutive mornings in the third week; release from home isolation and return to dental work when all three are negative, with continued clinical improvement
Sputum smear and culture monthly until two consecutive cultures are negative, including a culture at the end of the intensive phase
Continuation phase of isoniazid and rifampin for four months if the two-month culture is negative, or seven months if it is positive
No alcohol during treatment; counseling with a substance-use counselor; acamprosate if medication is wanted
Hepatitis B vaccination, which can wait until treatment ends

I will review the results by message at two months and at the end of treatment; no infectious diseases visit is needed unless the cultures stay positive, a drug must be stopped, or resistance is found
